statement: NBER's Business Cycle Dating Committee identified July 1980 as a business-cycle trough, reaffirming January 1980 as the prior peak; it called the six-month 1980 recession the shortest in its chronology since 1854.
label: 1980 recession
source_title: Business Cycle Dating Committee Announcement July 8, 1981
publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)
support: identified July 1980 as the most recent trough in the US business cycle
notes: Dates are NBER peak and trough months; NBER counts the months after the peak through the trough as recession. National event: local changes in these months are coincident unless local sources document a link.

statement: NBER's Business Cycle Dating Committee identified November 1982 as the trough of the recession that began in July 1981; it noted the recession's sixteen-month length equaled that of the 1973-75 recession.
label: 1981-82 recession
source_title: Business Cycle Dating Committee Announcement July 8, 1983
publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)
support: identified November 1982 as the trough of the recession that had begun
notes: Dates are NBER peak and trough months; NBER counts the months after the peak through the trough as recession. National event: local changes in these months are coincident unless local sources document a link.

statement: NBER's Business Cycle Dating Committee determined that US economic activity peaked in July 1990 and reached a trough in March 1991; the eight months between them are a recession in NBER's chronology.

publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)
support: The eight-month period between July 1990 and March 1991 is a recession
notes: Dates are NBER peak and trough months; NBER counts the months after the peak through the trough as recession. National event: local changes in these months are coincident unless local sources document a link.

statement: NBER's Business Cycle Dating Committee determined that a November 2001 trough ended the recession that began in March 2001; the recession lasted 8 months.

publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)
support: The trough marks the end of the recession that began in March 2001
notes: Dates are NBER peak and trough months; NBER counts the months after the peak through the trough as recession. National event: local changes in these months are coincident unless local sources document a link.

statement: NBER's Business Cycle Dating Committee determined that a June 2009 trough ended the recession that began in December 2007; at 18 months it was the longest recession since World War II.

publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)
support: The trough marks the end of the recession that began in December 2007

statement: NBER's Business Cycle Dating Committee determined a February 2020 peak and an April 2020 trough; the two-month recession is the shortest US recession on record.

NBER's Business Cycle Dating page still listed Feb 2020/Apr 2020 as the most recent peak/trough on 2026-09-28.

statement: The 2020 Census used improved designs for its separate Hispanic origin and race questions and updated data processing and coding; the Census Bureau says 2020-2010 race comparisons should be made with caution.

statement: According to the Census Bureau, it did not release standard 2020 ACS 1-year estimates because of COVID-19 impacts on data collection, which produced nonresponse bias; limited experimental estimates were released November 30, 2021.
